items.title: Evolution & Committees on Panchayati Raj
items.body:
**In one line**
Local self-government in India grew from British-era experiments and a string of expert committees before it finally won a place in the Constitution in 1992.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC/UPSC repeatedly test "which committee recommended what" and "who started local self-government", so the sequence and the key names are high-value.

**The story**
- **British roots**: **Mayo's Resolution (1870)** began financial decentralisation; **Lord Ripon's Resolution (1882)** — the **'Magna Carta' of local self-government** — mandated elected members and non-official chairpersons. The **Royal Commission on Decentralisation (1907)**, chaired by **C.E.H. Hobhouse**, stressed village panchayats, and the **Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms (1919)** made local government a transferred provincial subject.
- **After independence**: **Article 40 (a Directive Principle)** directed the State to organise village panchayats, but being non-justiciable it produced no uniformity, and **B.R. Ambedkar** was sceptical of panchayats. The **Community Development Programme (1952)** and **National Extension Service (1953)** underperformed for lack of people's participation.
- **The committees** that shaped reform:

| Committee | Year | Core recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| Balwant Rai Mehta | 1957 | **Three-tier** PRI (Village–Block–District) |
| Ashok Mehta | 1977 | **Two-tier** (Zilla Parishad + Mandal Panchayat) |
| G.V.K. Rao | 1985 | District as the **basic unit of planning** |
| L.M. Singhvi | 1986 | **Constitutional status** for PRIs |
| P.K. Thungon | 1989 | Constitutional recognition |

**Rajasthan** launched PRIs first (**2 October 1959**, Nagaur), followed by **Andhra Pradesh (1 November 1959)**.

**Terms explained**
- **Decentralisation** — handing powers and funds down from the Centre/State to local bodies.
- **Directive Principle (DPSP)** — a goal the Constitution asks the State to pursue, but which courts cannot enforce.
- **Non-justiciable** — not enforceable in a court.

**Don't confuse**
- **Balwant Rai Mehta = three-tier; Ashok Mehta = two-tier** — do not swap them.
- **L.M. Singhvi (constitutional status)** vs **G.V.K. Rao (district planning)** — a frequent match-the-pair trap.

**Remember it**
Committee order by year: Balwant ('57) → Ashok ('77) → GVK Rao ('85) → Singhvi ('86) → Thungon ('89).

**TL;DR**
- Ripon 1882 = 'Magna Carta' of local self-government; Mayo 1870 began financial decentralisation.
- Article 40 (DPSP) directed village panchayats; non-justiciable.
- Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) = three-tier; Ashok Mehta (1977) = two-tier; Singhvi (1986) = constitutional status.
- Rajasthan launched PRIs first (2 Oct 1959), then Andhra Pradesh (1 Nov 1959).
keyPoints: Ripon's Resolution of 1882 is the 'Magna Carta' of local self-government; Mayo's 1870 Resolution began financial decentralisation.
Royal Commission on Decentralisation (1907) was chaired by C.E.H. Hobhouse.
Article 40 (DPSP) directs the State to organise village panchayats; it is non-justiciable.
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended the three-tier system; Ashok Mehta (1977) the two-tier system.
L.M. Singhvi (1986) recommended constitutional status for PRIs.
Rajasthan launched PRIs first (2 Oct 1959), followed by Andhra Pradesh (1 Nov 1959).

items.title: 73rd & 74th Amendments — Structure, Reservation, Tenure
items.body:
**In one line**
Two 1992 amendments — the 73rd for villages and the 74th for towns — finally made local governments a permanent, elected third tier of India's federal system.

**Why it is asked**
The Part/Schedule/Article numbers, the 29-vs-18 figures and the reservation and tenure rules are among the most heavily tested polity facts.

**The story**
- **73rd Amendment** → **Part IX ('The Panchayats')**, Articles **243–243O**, the **Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects)**. In force **24 April 1993** (National Panchayati Raj Day).
- **74th Amendment** → **Part IXA ('The Municipalities')**, Articles **243P–243ZG**, the **Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects)**. In force **1 June 1993**.
- **Structure**: three tiers — Village (**Gram Panchayat**) → Intermediate (**Block/Mandal/Taluk**) → District (**Zilla Parishad**). The intermediate tier is **optional** for a State with population **not exceeding 20 lakh** (Art 243B). The **Gram Sabha** (Art 243A) — all registered voters of a village — is the base deliberative unit, and all seats are filled by **direct election** (Art 243C).
- **Reservation and tenure**: **SC/ST** seats are reserved **in proportion to population**; **women** get **not less than one-third** of seats and chairperson posts (Art 243D), and many States, including AP, have raised this to **50%**. Panchayats have a **five-year term** (Art 243E), with elections before expiry or within **6 months** of dissolution. Elections are run by the **State Election Commission** (Art 243K), NOT the Election Commission of India.

**Terms explained**
- **Eleventh / Twelfth Schedule** — lists of subjects the State *may* hand to panchayats (29) and municipalities (18).
- **Gram Sabha** — the village assembly of all adult voters.
- **State Election Commission** — a State body that runs local-body polls.

**Don't confuse**
- **73rd = Rural / 29 subjects / Eleventh Schedule** vs **74th = Urban / 18 subjects / Twelfth Schedule** — do not flip the numbers.
- **State Election Commission (local bodies) is NOT the Election Commission of India** (Parliament/Assembly polls).

**Remember it**
73 = Rural (Panchayats, 11th Schedule, 29); 74 = Urban (Municipalities, 12th Schedule, 18).

**TL;DR**
- 73rd: Part IX, Arts 243–243O, Eleventh Schedule (29), in force 24 Apr 1993.
- 74th: Part IXA, Arts 243P–243ZG, Twelfth Schedule (18), in force 1 Jun 1993.
- Three tiers; intermediate tier optional below 20 lakh population (Art 243B).
- Women ≥ one-third (Art 243D); 5-year term (Art 243E); State Election Commission conducts polls (Art 243K).
keyPoints: 73rd Amendment = Part IX, Arts 243–243O, Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects), in force 24 Apr 1993.
74th Amendment = Part IXA, Arts 243P–243ZG, Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects), in force 1 Jun 1993.
Three-tier structure; intermediate tier optional for states with population ≤ 20 lakh (Art 243B).
One-third of seats and chairperson posts reserved for women (Art 243D); SC/ST reservation is population-proportional.
Panchayats have a five-year term (Art 243E); elections run by the State Election Commission (Art 243K).

items.title: Articles 243–243ZG & the Schedules — Quick Reference
items.body:
**In one line**
Parts IX and IXA pack the whole local-government scheme into a short run of numbered Articles, and the exam picks single Articles out of this list.

**Why it is asked**
Match-the-Article questions (243A, 243D, 243I, 243K, 243ZD) are common, so you must be able to attach each number to its provision.

**The story**
The Constitution assigns one job to each Article so that powers, elections and finances all have a clear home.

Panchayats — **Part IX (Arts 243–243O)**:

| Article | Provision |
|---|---|
| 243A | Gram Sabha |
| 243B | Constitution of Panchayats (3 tiers) |
| 243C | Composition |
| 243D | Reservation of seats (SC/ST/women) |
| 243E | Duration — 5 years |
| 243G | Powers, authority and responsibilities |
| 243H | Power to impose taxes; funds |
| 243I | State Finance Commission |
| 243K | State Election Commission |
| 243M | Part not to apply to certain (Scheduled) areas |

Municipalities — **Part IXA (Arts 243P–243ZG)**:

| Article | Provision |
|---|---|
| 243Q | Three types of municipalities |
| 243R | Composition |
| 243T | Reservation of seats |
| 243W | Powers and functions |
| 243Y | State Finance Commission (municipalities) |
| 243ZA | Elections (State Election Commission) |
| 243ZD | District Planning Committee |
| 243ZE | Metropolitan Planning Committee |

The **Eleventh Schedule** carries 29 functional items for panchayats; the **Twelfth Schedule** carries 18 for municipalities.

**Terms explained**
- **State Finance Commission (243I/243Y)** — reviews, every five years, how money is shared with local bodies.
- **District Planning Committee (243ZD)** — merges the plans of panchayats and municipalities in a district.
- **Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE)** — the same idea for a large metro area.

**Don't confuse**
- **243I = State Finance Commission** vs **243K = State Election Commission** — money versus elections.
- **243ZD (District Planning)** vs **243ZE (Metropolitan Planning)** — district versus metro.

**Remember it**
A-B-C-D-E … I, K: gram-sabhA, Bodies, Composition, reservation-D, duration-E, finance-I, election-K.

**TL;DR**
- 243A = Gram Sabha; 243B = three tiers; 243D = reservation; 243E = 5-year duration.
- 243G = powers/planning; 243H = taxes; 243I = State Finance Commission; 243K = State Election Commission.
- 243ZD = District Planning Committee; 243ZE = Metropolitan Planning Committee.
- Eleventh Schedule = 29 (panchayats); Twelfth Schedule = 18 (municipalities).
keyPoints: 243A = Gram Sabha; 243B = constitution of the three tiers.
243D = reservation; 243E = five-year duration; 243G = powers/planning; 243H = taxes.
243I = State Finance Commission; 243K = State Election Commission for panchayats.
243ZD = District Planning Committee; 243ZE = Metropolitan Planning Committee (Part IXA).
Eleventh Schedule = 29 subjects (panchayats); Twelfth Schedule = 18 subjects (municipalities).
items.mnemonic: 'A B C D E … I K' — Gram sabhA, Bodies, Composition, reservation-D, duration-E, finance-I, election-K.

items.title: PESA Act 1996 & Scheduled Areas
items.body:
**In one line**
PESA, 1996 carries the panchayat system into India's tribal (Fifth Schedule) areas, but reshapes it so that the Gram Sabha — not the higher tiers — holds real power.

**Why it is asked**
The Fifth-vs-Sixth Schedule distinction and "what PESA empowers the Gram Sabha to do" are classic traps.

**The story**
Ordinary **Part IX does not automatically apply to the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled) areas (Article 243M)**, because tribal society needs rules fitted to its customs. Parliament therefore passed the **Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA)**.

PESA extends panchayat provisions to **Fifth Schedule areas across ten States** (including **Andhra Pradesh**) and makes the **Gram Sabha the centre of tribal self-governance**. The Gram Sabha approves development plans and beneficiary lists, manages **minor forest produce, minor water bodies and land**, must be consulted before land acquisition and resettlement, and safeguards **tribal customs and traditions**. PESA also stops higher-tier panchayats from encroaching on the powers of lower tiers.

Several regions stay **outside Part IX**: Fifth Schedule areas (covered instead by PESA), **Sixth Schedule** tribal areas of the North-East, the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram, and hill areas such as Darjeeling.

**Terms explained**
- **Fifth Schedule** — the Constitution's framework for Scheduled areas in mainland States (where PESA applies).
- **Sixth Schedule** — a separate framework for tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram (autonomous district councils).
- **Minor forest produce** — non-timber forest items (bamboo, tendu leaves, honey) that tribals may own and sell.

**Don't confuse**
- **PESA covers the Fifth Schedule, NOT the Sixth Schedule** (North-East) — the single most common error.
- PESA aims at **self-governance within the State**, not at creating autonomous regions.

**Remember it**
PESA = Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas — Fifth (not Sixth) Schedule.

**TL;DR**
- Part IX does not automatically apply to Fifth Schedule areas (Art 243M).
- PESA, 1996 extends panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas in ten States, including AP.
- It makes the Gram Sabha central to tribal self-rule and resource/custom protection.
- PESA = Fifth Schedule; the Sixth Schedule (North-East) is a different system.
keyPoints: Part IX does not automatically apply to Fifth Schedule areas (Article 243M).
PESA Act, 1996 = Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act.
PESA extends panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas in ten states, including Andhra Pradesh.
It makes the Gram Sabha central to tribal self-rule and protection of customs and resources.
PESA covers the Fifth Schedule, NOT the Sixth Schedule (North-East) areas.
items.mnemonic: PESA = Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas — Fifth (not Sixth) Schedule.

items.title: Urban Local Bodies (74th Amendment)
items.body:
**In one line**
The 74th Amendment gives towns and cities their own elected governments, graded by size from a Nagar Panchayat up to a Municipal Corporation.

**Why it is asked**
The three types under Article 243Q, the Twelfth Schedule figure and the "first corporation" fact are standard one-mark questions.

**The story**
Urban self-government rests on **Part IXA** and the **Twelfth Schedule (18 items)**; India's first municipal corporation was set up at **Madras in 1688**. **Article 243Q** classifies municipalities into three types by the size of the area:

| Body | Constituted for | Head |
|---|---|---|
| **Nagar Panchayat** | Area **in transition** from rural to urban | Chairperson |
| **Municipal Council** | Smaller urban area | President / Chairperson |
| **Municipal Corporation** | Larger urban area | Mayor |

Besides these elected bodies, several **administrative urban bodies** exist outside Art 243Q: the **Notified Area Committee** (a developing town, with all members nominated), **Town Area Committee** (a small town, limited powers), **Cantonment Board** (set up and controlled by the **central government** for the civilian population near military stations), **Township**, **Port Trust** and **Special Purpose Agency**.

Two planning bodies tie the levels together: the **District Planning Committee (Art 243ZD)** consolidates panchayat and municipal plans, and the **Metropolitan Planning Committee (Art 243ZE)** does this for metros with a population of 10 lakh or more.

**Terms explained**
- **Nagar Panchayat** — the municipal body for a place turning from rural into urban.
- **Cantonment Board** — a civic body for a military-station town, run under the central government.
- **Metropolitan area** — an urban area of 10 lakh or more people spread over one or more districts.

**Don't confuse**
- **Nagar Panchayat (transitional area) vs Gram Panchayat (village)** — one is urban-in-the-making, the other is rural.
- **Only a Municipal Corporation is headed by a Mayor**; the smaller bodies have Chairpersons/Presidents.

**Remember it**
Urban ladder by size: Nagar Panchayat < Municipal Council < Municipal Corporation.

**TL;DR**
- Part IXA + Twelfth Schedule (18 items); first corporation at Madras, 1688.
- Article 243Q: Nagar Panchayat (transitional), Municipal Council (smaller), Municipal Corporation (larger, Mayor).
- Cantonment Boards are controlled by the central government.
- 243ZD (District) and 243ZE (Metropolitan) Planning Committees integrate area plans.
keyPoints: Part IXA + Twelfth Schedule (18 items) govern municipalities; first corporation at Madras, 1688.
Article 243Q gives three types: Nagar Panchayat (transitional), Municipal Council (smaller), Municipal Corporation (larger).
A Municipal Corporation is headed by a Mayor.
Cantonment Boards are set up and controlled by the central government.
District Planning Committee (243ZD) and Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE) integrate area plans.
items.mnemonic: Urban ladder by size: Nagar Panchayat < Municipal Council < Municipal Corporation.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh — PR Act 1994, Mandal System & Sachivalayams
items.body:
**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh runs a three-tier panchayat system under its 1994 Act and has added the Grama/Ward Sachivalayam layer (2019) to bring government services to people's doorsteps.

**Why it is asked**
AP-specific institutions — the mandal tier, the 1994 Act and the Sachivalayam-Volunteer model — are prime material for the APPSC State paper.

**The story**
- **AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 (Act 13 of 1994)** consolidated the State's laws on Gram Panchayats, Mandal Parishads and Zilla Parishads and gave effect to the **73rd Amendment**. AP's three tiers are **Gram Panchayat (Sarpanch) → Mandal Praja Parishad (President) → Zilla Praja Parishad (Chairperson)**. The **mandal** replaced the older block/taluk as the intermediate tier in AP, introduced in the 1980s under **N.T. Rama Rao**.
- **Grama/Ward Sachivalayam system (2019)**: launched on **2 October 2019** for corruption-free, doorstep governance. About **15,004 Grama Sachivalayams** (rural) and **3,842 Ward Sachivalayams** (urban) were set up, each staffed by dedicated functionaries delivering hundreds of government services locally. They are backed by **Grama/Ward Volunteers**, each serving roughly **50 households**, for last-mile delivery of welfare (Direct Benefit Transfer) schemes. This layer is **administrative** and complements — it does **not** replace — the constitutional **Gram Sabha / Panchayat**.
- AP also has **Fifth Schedule areas**, so **PESA, 1996** applies in its tribal (Scheduled) regions.

**Terms explained**
- **Mandal Praja Parishad** — AP's intermediate (block-level) tier, headed by an MPP President.
- **Grama Sachivalayam** — a village secretariat of government staff for single-window service delivery.
- **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)** — paying welfare benefits straight into a beneficiary's bank account.

**Don't confuse**
- A **Gram Panchayat is headed by a Sarpanch**, not a Mayor (a Mayor heads a municipal corporation).
- The **Sachivalayam is an administrative layer**; it does not abolish the elected Gram Sabha/Panchayat.

**Remember it**
AP tiers G-M-Z: Gram → Mandal → Zilla; the Sachivalayam started on Gandhi Jayanti, 2 October 2019.

**TL;DR**
- AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 implemented the 73rd Amendment; tiers = Gram Panchayat → Mandal Praja Parishad → Zilla Praja Parishad.
- The mandal is AP's intermediate tier, from the 1980s under N.T. Rama Rao.
- Grama/Ward Sachivalayam (2 Oct 2019): ~15,004 Grama + 3,842 Ward secretariats, Volunteers for ~50 households each.
- It is administrative and does not replace the Gram Sabha; PESA applies in AP's Fifth Schedule areas.
keyPoints: AP Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 (Act 13 of 1994) implemented the 73rd Amendment and consolidated PRI laws in the state.
AP's three tiers: Gram Panchayat (Sarpanch), Mandal Praja Parishad (President), Zilla Praja Parishad (Chairperson).
The mandal is AP's intermediate tier, introduced in the 1980s under N.T. Rama Rao.
The Grama/Ward Sachivalayam system was launched on 2 October 2019 for doorstep governance.
About 15,004 Grama and 3,842 Ward Sachivalayams operate, backed by Volunteers each serving ~50 households.
The Sachivalayam is administrative and does not replace the constitutional Gram Sabha; PESA applies in AP's Fifth Schedule areas.
items.mnemonic: AP tiers G-M-Z: Gram → Mandal → Zilla; Sachivalayam started on Gandhi Jayanti 2019.

items.title: PYQ Precision — Age, Tenure & SVAMITVA
items.body:
**In one line**
A few precise facts — the minimum age of 21, the "remainder of term" rule, and the drone-based SVAMITVA scheme — decide several previous-year questions.

**Why it is asked**
These are direct UPSC/APPSC previous-year items where one swapped number (21 vs 25) or one wrong ministry flips the answer.

**The story**
- **Age and tenure**: the **minimum age to be a Panchayat member is 21 years** (Art 243F) — NOT 25 (25 is for the Lok Sabha). The **term is 5 years** (Art 243E), with elections within **6 months** of dissolution. A Panchayat reconstituted after **premature dissolution** serves only the **remainder** of the original term; one that completes its full term gets a fresh 5 years.
- **SVAMITVA Scheme (2020–21)**: the name stands for **S**urvey of **V**illages **A**nd **M**apping with **I**mprovised **T**echnology in **V**illage **A**reas. It uses **drones** to survey **abadi (inhabited) rural land** and issues **property cards** (a record of rights) to household owners. It is implemented by the **Ministry of Panchayati Raj**, and the property cards help owners access institutional credit and reduce land disputes.

**Terms explained**
- **Abadi land** — the inhabited (built-up) part of a village, as opposed to farmland.
- **Property card** — an official document proving ownership of a house/plot.
- **Record of rights** — the government's register of who owns which land.

**Don't confuse**
- **Panchayat member minimum age = 21** (Art 243F), not 25.
- A Panchayat after **premature dissolution** serves only the **leftover term**, not a fresh five years.
- **SVAMITVA is run by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj**, not the Ministry of Rural Development.

**Remember it**
21 to stand for a Panchayat; SVAMITVA = drones + property cards under the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.

**TL;DR**
- Minimum age to be a Panchayat member = 21 years (Art 243F).
- Term = 5 years (Art 243E); elections within 6 months of dissolution.
- After premature dissolution, a Panchayat serves only the remainder of the original term.
- SVAMITVA (2020-21): drones survey abadi land and issue property cards; run by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.
keyPoints: Minimum age to be a Panchayat member is 21 years (Art 243F), not 25.
Panchayat term is 5 years (Art 243E); elections within 6 months of dissolution.
A body reconstituted after premature dissolution serves only the remainder of the original term.
SVAMITVA (2020-21) uses drones to survey abadi land and issues property cards.
SVAMITVA is implemented by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.
items.source: UPSC 2016 Prelims (Rau's IAS COMPASS); Constitution Arts 243E/243F; Ministry of Panchayati Raj / PIB (SVAMITVA)

items.title: For Mains — Panchayati Raj & Local Government
items.body:
Mains (GS-3, clause M3-3: Rural & Urban Local Governance) asks you to **judge** how far the 73rd/74th Amendments delivered real self-government, not to list Article numbers. Build answers on these dimensions.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| **Promise** | Constitutional third tier; three-tier structure; reserved seats (women one-third → 50% in AP); SEC (243K), SFC (243I); Eleventh/Twelfth Schedules |
| **Gaps** | Devolution of the **3 Fs** (funds, functions, functionaries) is discretionary (Art 243G); thin own-revenue; SFC advice non-binding; staff deputed, not dedicated |
| **Social deficits** | Proxy representation ("Sarpanch-Pati"), elite/line-department capture, MLA/MP interference, weak Gram Sabhas |
| **Significance** | Deepens democracy, local planning, welfare delivery, women's leadership; PESA empowers tribal Gram Sabhas |
| **Way forward** | 2nd ARC "activity mapping", untied funds, separate panchayat cadre (Karnataka), enforceable SFC, capacity-building |

**Data points / reports / schemes to quote**
- **2nd ARC, 6th report** — "Local Governance: An Inspiring Journey into the Future" (subsidiarity, activity mapping).
- **PESA, 1996** — Gram Sabha control over minor forest produce, land and consent in Fifth Schedule areas.
- **SVAMITVA (2020-21)** — drone survey + property cards (Ministry of Panchayati Raj).
- **Finance Commission** grants-in-aid to local bodies (Art 280 reads with Art 243I).
- Model States: **Kerala** (People's Plan Campaign) and **Karnataka** (strong devolution, separate cadre).

**AP angle**
AP's **Grama/Ward Sachivalayam + Volunteer model (2 Oct 2019)** is a strong doorstep-delivery innovation, but as an administrative layer it must reinforce — not overshadow — the elected Gram Panchayat/Gram Sabha. AP's **28 Zilla Praja Parishads** (effective 25 Sep 2026, one per district) and **Fifth Schedule PESA areas** give ready State examples.

**Use in answers**
- *Example*: contrast Kerala's People's Plan with the national "3 Fs" shortfall.
- *Quote*: Gandhi's vision of "village republics" (Gram Swaraj) as the aspiration.
- *Diagram idea*: a pyramid — Gram Sabha at the base, Gram Panchayat, Mandal/Block, Zilla Parishad — with "funds + functions + functionaries" as the three supports.
keyPoints: Judge the 73rd/74th Amendments on promise vs the discretionary devolution of the 3 Fs (Art 243G).
Core gaps: thin finances, non-binding SFC, deputed staff, proxy representation and capture.
Quote the 2nd ARC 6th report (activity mapping), PESA 1996 and the SVAMITVA scheme.
Model States Kerala (People's Plan) and Karnataka (separate cadre) show what real devolution achieves.
AP angle: Grama/Ward Sachivalayam (2019) must reinforce, not overshadow, elected panchayats; 28 ZPPs from 25 Sep 2026.
Way forward: untied funds, enforceable SFC, dedicated cadre, stronger Gram Sabhas.
